strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for NLP: how serialization of structured information affects LLM reasoning. Comparing reordered descriptions of the same graphs is an appropriate starting point for studying this sensitivity.

The reported traversal-order gains are substantial. In Table 1, BFS raises average connectivity accuracy from 78.36% to 89.43%, while DFS raises Hamilton-path accuracy from 31.50% to 52.43%. These results support a useful empirical observation independently of the proposed explanations.

The study includes five structural tasks, node classification on three citation networks, five prompting styles, and partial replication on five additional models. The task-dependent ordering preferences provide more insight than a single aggregate improvement.
weaknesses: The PPR comparisons contain important methodological issues. Appendix A.2 uses an existing cycle or the correct shortest path to construct personalization vectors, making these orders answer-informed interventions that should be identified as oracle conditions. For Hamilton paths, the path contains every vertex, so the stated personalization is uniform and should produce ordinary PageRank rankings. The different PR and PPR results in Table 1 therefore require reconciliation, including any tie-breaking or run variability.

Section 5 does not establish improved graph understanding beyond answer overlap. Accuracy below 100% when the correct path guides ordering cannot rule out imperfect exploitation of that ordering as the entire source of improvement. Controls matching answer overlap while varying structural organization are needed. The positional-encoding and attention explanations also remain hypotheses without direct experimental support.

The central ordering procedure is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 3.2 switches from node traversal to traversal of an undefined 'dual graph' without explaining its construction or the mapping back to ordered edges. Root selection, neighbor ordering, and tie-breaking need precise specifications. The manuscript also lacks a dataset/code access link, graph-generation seeds, edge-weight distribution, and a complete specification of the prompts used in each condition.

Evaluation reliability is not adequately demonstrated. Appendix A.3 uses string-based parsing for GPT responses but an unspecified GPT judge for the additional models, without judge prompts or validation against deterministic graph checks. This particularly affects tasks with multiple valid paths or topological orders. The experiments also provide no confidence intervals or paired significance tests, despite repeated claims of significant improvements; node classification uses only 50 graphs per dataset/sampling condition, repeated three times.

The task-level explanations contain errors and overinterpretation. BFS does not guarantee a minimum-weight path in the weighted shortest-path setting evaluated here. Connectivity and cycle detection can also require global traversal. Figure 4 measures variance across aggregate accuracies for five ordering methods; this does not establish per-instance robustness to permutations or isolate task complexity from differences in baseline accuracy and output requirements.

The broad conclusions exceed the demonstrated scope: structural experiments use 5–15-node Erdős–Rényi graphs at one density and one encoding, with the comprehensive evaluation concentrated on GPT-3.5. Simple lexicographic or adjacency-grouped controls would help distinguish traversal-specific benefits from basic edge grouping. The promising ordering effect warrants further work, but the unresolved implementation, evaluation, and interpretation issues require important revisions before a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation.
